To shriek means to make a very loud, high-pitched, sharp cry or sound that bursts out suddenly and involuntarily. It's not just any loud sound — it has a specific quality: high in pitch, piercing (meaning it cuts sharply through other sounds), and uncontrolled.

Think of the sound a person makes when something suddenly scares them — that instant, sharp, high sound that escapes before they even decide to make it. That's a shriek.
The two key qualities that define shrieking

Understanding these two qualities will help you recognize and use the word correctly:

1. High-pitched — A shriek is never a deep or low sound. It's sharp and high, the kind of sound that goes straight to your ears.

2. Involuntary and uncontrolled — This is crucial. People don't choose to shriek the way they choose to speak. It bursts out of them, driven by overwhelming emotion. This sense of losing control is built into the word.

Shrieking is triggered by extreme emotions — the kind that are so powerful that the sound simply escapes a person:

  • Sudden fear or terror — This is the most classic use. Someone sees something frightening, and they shriek.
  • Sudden shock or surprise — Even something unexpected (not necessarily scary) can cause a shriek.
  • Extreme pain — A sharp, sudden pain can make someone shriek.
  • Extreme excitement or delight — Children very commonly shriek when they're wildly excited. The same high-pitched, uncontrolled quality appears here too.
  • Uncontrolled laughter — The phrase "shrieked with laughter" is very common. It means laughing so hard and freely that your laughter becomes high-pitched and unrestrained.

People shriek most commonly. But the word goes beyond humans:

  • Animals — Birds, monkeys, and certain other animals shriek. A bird of prey, for example, can shriek.
  • Wind — Writers often say the wind shrieks during a fierce storm. This is a creative use, giving the wind a human-like quality, and it perfectly captures that sharp, high-pitched howl of a strong wind.
  • Machines or objects — Brakes, tyres, or metal surfaces can shriek — meaning they produce that same sharp, piercing, high-pitched sound.
How to use it in a sentence

Intransitive (shrieking without saying words):

  • She shrieked when the dog jumped at her.
  • The children shrieked with excitement at the carnival.
  • He shrieked in pain and dropped the knife.

Transitive (shrieking actual words out):

  • "Get out!" she shrieked.
  • She shrieked his name across the hallway.
  • "Run!" he shrieked as the wall collapsed.

With "with" (to describe the emotion driving the shriek):

  • shriek with fear
  • shriek with laughter
  • shriek with delight
  • shriek with excitement

"At" someone (directed shrieking, often out of anger or panic):

  • She shrieked at him to stop the car.
  • The crowd shrieked at the performer.
How shriek is different from similar words

This is important, because words like scream, yell, and cry are close — but not identical:

Shriek vs. Scream:
These are the most similar. The difference is subtle but real. A scream can be deep or high-pitched, and it can be long and sustained. A shriek is specifically high-pitched and tends to be sharper and more sudden — like a single piercing burst. You can imagine a prolonged scream of terror, but a shriek is more like an explosive moment of sound.

Shriek vs. Yell/Shout:
Yelling and shouting are loud, but they are deliberate and controlled. You choose to yell at someone. You never really "choose" to shriek — it's involuntary. Also, yelling is usually not high-pitched; shrieking always is.

Shriek vs. Cry:
"Cry" is a very broad word — it can mean weeping, or any kind of calling out. Shrieking is a specific, high-pitched, piercing burst. All shrieks could loosely be called cries, but most cries are not shrieks.

Shriek vs. Squeal:
A squeal is also high-pitched and uncontrolled, but it's lighter and often associated with milder emotions — a little surprise, mild excitement, playful delight. A shriek is more intense, more forceful, and suggests a stronger emotional charge.

Shriek vs. Wail:
A wail is a prolonged, mournful cry — lower, sustained, associated with grief and sorrow. A shriek is sharp and sudden. The two are very different in character.

When you read or hear the word shriek, it creates an immediate sensory impact. It is vivid and expressive. Good writers choose this word precisely because it communicates not just that a sound was made, but what kind of sound — sharp, high, forceful, out of control. It makes the reader almost hear the sound.

It is a word that belongs to moments of intensity. Wherever you see it, something strong is happening — fear, shock, wild laughter, unbearable pain, overwhelming joy.
A quick summary to anchor everything

To shriek = to make a sudden, loud, high-pitched, piercing sound driven by overwhelming emotion — a sound that is not controlled or chosen, but simply escapes.

The emotion is usually extreme: terror, sudden shock, sharp pain, wild excitement, or helpless laughter. The sound is never deep or low. It is always sharp, high, and piercing. Humans shriek, some animals shriek, and even wind and machines are described as shrieking when they produce that same sharp, high, cutting sound.
